newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Disease kills 150 Hutus in Burundi relocation camp.
newsitem.headline: Disease kills 150 Hutus in Burundi relocation camp.

text.p: Disease has killed 150 Burundian Hutus grouped by government troops into a relocation camp at Ruhinga north of Bujumbura, occupants said on Thursday.
They said bacterial dysentery, diarrhoea and malaria were rampant among the 12,000 people brought from their villages and farms by the Tutsi-dominated army in its war with Hutu rebels.

"There are lots of sick, they can't leave and they don't have enough strength to reach the dispensaries," said 36-year -old camp resident Dominique Kambakeyo at Ruhinga, 120 km (75 miles) north of the capital.
As worsening violence in the brutal war with Hutu rebels has gripped the countryside the army has adopted a policy of relocating Hutu civilians to camps, officially to protect them.
Tutsis are outnumbered four-to-one in Burundi and many fear they will perish unless they retain full control of the army and block real power-sharing with Hutus in the tiny central African state.

"The rebels want the people to stay on the hillsides so they can hide amongst them, that's why we put them in the camps to protect them," said the army commander of Ruhinga Camp, Lieutenant Gaspard Ndambambarire, who warned of the worsening health situation there.
"If non-governmental organisations don't help, the government will have to be asked to take responsibility because a solution is essential, if not lots of people will die," he said.
Many of Ruhinga's occupants show few signs of wanting to stay there.
"When there is still insecurity it is difficult for us to return home, but here there is hunger, there is sickness and it is better to let us stay in our homes," said Oscar Minani.
Aid agencies say more than 150,000 people have been grouped in relocation camps in the past month. Ruhinga residents said the 150 had died of disease in the camp in the last three weeks.
Michele Hofman of Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF-Doctors Without Borders) Holland said there were five large relocation camps, the largest of which is Nyarurama with 50,000 people.
"I am sure that there is sickness and death, but I can't give any figures."
Political opponents of Burundi's military leader Pierre Buyoya accuse the army of establishing concentration camps.

"To protect people, you evacuate them from the battlefield, but when you put them together to exterminate them with sickness and hunger it's a funny kind of protection," said Augustin Nzojibwani, secretary general of the mainly Hutu FRODEBU party.

Buyoya last week promised to investigate reports by the United Nations that the army has killed at least 1,000 people since the start of December. More than 150,000 people have been killed since 1993 in the civil war and massacres by both sides.
Renegade Tutsi soldiers murdered Burundi's first freely -elected president, Melchior Ndadaye, a Hutu, in October 1993.
Neighbouring countries led by Tanzania imposed a transport and economic embargo on Burundi after Buyoya seized power last July in an attempt to force him to negotiate with Hutu rebels.
